notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Joshua 22, drawn from the sources I was able to consult.

---

## Joshua 22 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### vv. 1–4: Joshua Dismisses the Eastern Tribes with Commendation

**v. 1 — "Then Joshua summoned the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh…"**
- The war with the Canaanites being ended and the land divided, Joshua now releases the 2½ tribes who had crossed over to fight alongside their brethren. This is the first of three assemblies Joshua calls in the closing chapters (cf. 22:1; 23:2; 24:1), marking the "Consecration" section of the book. (preceptaustin.org)
- Gill notes that these tribes had, at their own request, received their portion east of Jordan, and Joshua now addresses them honourably after their faithful service. (studylight.org, Gill)

**v. 2 — "You have done all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, and you have obeyed my voice…"**
- Joshua gives a threefold commendation: they kept Moses' charge, obeyed Joshua, and (v. 3) did not forsake their brothers. The Hebrew verb *shama* ("listened/obeyed") implies hearing with attention that leads to action. (preceptaustin.org)
- Gill: This refers to their promise to leave families and flocks behind, cross Jordan armed, and fight until Canaan was subdued (Numbers 32). They "punctually observed" this. (studylight.org, Gill)

**v. 3 — "All this time you have not deserted your brothers, up to this very day…"**
- "These many days" may have been as long as fourteen years (seven for conquest, seven for land division), according to Jewish tradition cited by Gill. Even at minimum, it was about seven years of separation from their families. (studylight.org, Gill; preceptaustin.org)
- Dale Ralph Davis (quoted at preceptaustin.org): "There is much to commend the practice of commending God’s people when it may be done sincerely." Matthew Henry adds: though God must have all the glory, "yet instruments must not be altogether overlooked."
- The Pulpit Commentary observes that the Israelites' remarkable obedience during Joshua's leadership — "not one single complaint" — contrasts sharply with the wilderness wanderings and with the period of the Judges that follows. This internal consistency "is of itself no small pledge of the trustworthiness of the whole." (biblehub.com, Pulpit)

**v. 4 — "And now that the LORD your God has given your brothers rest as He promised them, you may return to your homes…"**
- "Rest" (*nuach*) means freedom from active warfare — a relative rest, since Canaanites remained in the land. Precept Austin notes this rest is picked up in Hebrews 4:8 to show that a better, final Sabbath rest remains for God's people in Christ (cf. Mt 11:28–30). (preceptaustin.org)
- The Pulpit Commentary notes the LXX translates "given rest" as κατέπαυσε, the very word used in Hebrews 4:8. (biblehub.com, Pulpit)
- David Guzik (Enduring Word): These soldiers had fought side-by-side with their western brethren for seven years. "Now that the land was conquered and fully distributed…the eastern tribes could go back to their families." (enduringword.com)

---

### vv. 5–6: Joshua's Exhortation and Blessing

**v. 5 — "But be very careful to observe the commandment and the law… to love the LORD your God, to walk in all His ways, to keep His commandments, to hold fast to Him, and to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul."**
- David Guzik highlights the order of these commands as crucial: *first* hear God, *then* love Him, *then* obey. "To mix this order up is to drift into heresy (loving without hearing) or legalism (obeying before loving)." (enduringword.com)
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that Joshua's language is "crowded together" from Deuteronomy (6:5; 10:12; 11:13, 22; 30:6, 16, 20), so that "obedience to God's commands may be the more deeply impressed on their hearts." It adds that while beginning with love, Joshua does not end there: "If love be genuine, it is the practical principle which produces diligent service." (biblehub.com, Pulpit)
- Gill: Joshua gave this exhortation because the eastern tribes would be "at a distance from the tabernacle, altar, and service of God, and might be under temptation to relinquish it." (studylight.org, Gill)
- Matthew Henry (concise): "Those who have the commandment have it in vain, unless they do the commandment; and it will not be done aright unless we take diligent heed." (preceptaustin.org, quoting MHCC)

**v. 6 — "So Joshua blessed them and sent them on their way, and they went to their homes."**
- Joshua understood they could not do what God required without His blessing (cf. Numbers 6:23–27). (enduringword.com)
- Gill suggests the blessing may have included gifts and presents bestowed on them. (studylight.org, Gill)

---

### vv. 7–9: The Eastern Tribes Depart with Great Wealth

**v. 7 — "(To the half-tribe of Manasseh Moses had given land in Bashan, and to the other half Joshua gave land on the west side…)"**
- The Pulpit Commentary notes this is a characteristic repetition of the author: four times the book repeats that Manasseh was divided into two halves with inheritance on both sides of Jordan. "The form belongs to the author; the matter…belongs to God." (biblehub.com, Pulpit)
- Gill suggests the western half-tribe of Manasseh received a separate, more affectionate dismissal and blessing because Joshua himself was of the tribe of Ephraim, Manasseh's brother-tribe. (studylight.org, Gill)

**v. 8 — "Return to your homes with your great wealth… Divide with your brothers the spoil of your enemies."**
- Their obedience was rewarded with abundant spoil. Adam Clarke (quoted by Enduring Word): "It was right that those who stayed at home to defend the families…should have a proper proportion of the spoils." (enduringword.com)
- Gill notes the spoil included cattle, silver, gold, bronze, iron, and rich clothing taken from the Canaanites. He favours the view that "your brethren" refers to the other half-tribe of Manasseh remaining in Canaan, who should receive their share of the spoil. (studylight.org, Gill)
- The Pulpit Commentary observes the "strict and scrupulous integrity of Joshua" in dividing the spoil: unlike other leaders, "each man has his due, and no room is left for reproach or dissatisfaction." (biblehub.com, Pulpit)

**v. 9 — "So the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh left the Israelites at Shiloh…"**
- Shiloh was both the camp of Israel and the location of the tabernacle at this time. The mention of Shiloh "in the land of Canaan" distinguishes it from Gilead, the land east of Jordan. (biblehub.com, Pulpit; studylight.org, Gill)

---

### v. 10: The Eastern Tribes Build an Imposing Altar

**v. 10 — "…the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh built an imposing altar there by the Jordan."**
- The phrase "a great, impressive altar" is literally "an altar large in appearance" (Madvig, quoted at Enduring Word). It had to be large enough to be easily seen, because its function was to be a witness. (enduringword.com)
- The Pulpit Commentary discusses an identification of the site with Kurn Sartabeh (a prominent hill near the Jordan Valley), visible for many miles, though admits the evidence is uncertain. (biblehub.com, Pulpit)
- Ellicott: The Hebrew has "the altar" rather than "an altar" — it was a representation or copy of the altar of Jehovah at Shiloh. (biblehub.com, Ellicott)

---

### vv. 11–12: The Western Tribes Prepare for War

**v. 11 — "Then the Israelites received the report: 'Behold…they have built an altar on the border of the land of Canaan, at Geliloth near the Jordan on the Israelite side.'"**
- Ellicott translates: "Have built *the* altar" — it was a copy of Jehovah's altar, not a rival one. (biblehub.com, Ellicott)
- Gill argues the altar was actually on the *eastern* side, since "over against the land of Canaan" means opposite Canaan, and v. 11 clearly places it "at the passage of the children of Israel" — i.e., where they crossed, which was the ford by Jericho. (studylight.org, Gill)

**v. 12 — "And when they heard this, the whole congregation of Israel assembled at Shiloh to go to war against them."**
- David Guzik: "There was no discussion, there was an immediate reaction." The western tribes' rapid mobilization shows "spiritual health: a community willing to police itself for God's holiness, even at great cost to themselves." He adds this was "a healthy organism at work, able to purge itself of poisons." (enduringword.com)
- The Pulpit Commentary notes it is not Joshua who summons them — they gather voluntarily. This demonstrates the vivid sense of gratitude for their recent triumphs and the "strong, if short-lived, feeling of…indignation against his foes." The commentator argues this is evidence for the genuineness of the narrative: such zeal only makes sense after the catalogue of "splendid victories and wonderful Divine interpositions" recorded in the book. (biblehub.com, Pulpit)
- The law behind their action: Deuteronomy 13:12–16 commanded Israel to wage war against any Israelite city or tribe that turned to idolatry. (biblehub.com, Pulpit; studylight.org, Gill)

---

### vv. 13–15: A Delegation Is Sent Before War

**v. 13 — "The Israelites sent Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest…"**
- The Pulpit Commentary calls Phinehas "well chosen": he was the representative of the high priest, with a proven record of "fiery zeal for the purity of Israelitish faith" at Peor (Numbers 25:7). "Such an envoy, if the trans-Jordanic tribes had indeed disobeyed God's command, was well qualified to bring them to a sense of their sin." (biblehub.com, Pulpit)
- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary notes: "Trouble was averted because cool heads sought out reason before resorting to war, and because God’s man took the initiative." (studylight.org, Garner-Howes)

**v. 14 — "With him they sent ten chiefs—one family leader from each tribe of Israel…"**
- This was a high-ranking deputation: the son of the high priest plus ten princes, heads of tribes. The western half-tribe of Manasseh was also represented. The weight of the delegation befitted an embassy that might have to announce extermination. (biblehub.com, Pulpit; studylight.org, Gill)

**v. 15 — "They went to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh in the land of Gilead and said to them…"**
- The delegation either sent for the eastern chiefs or found them assembled. Phinehas was likely the spokesman. (studylight.org, Gill)

---

### vv. 16–20: The Accusation

**v. 16 — "'What is this breach of faith you have committed today against the God of Israel…?'"**
- The delegation speaks as "the whole congregation of the LORD" — not merely of Israel, but of the LORD, because "it was not on a civil but religious account they were come." (studylight.org, Gill)
- Guzik: "Clearly, the leadership of Israel thought that the altar at the Jordan represented a rival place of sacrifice and worship." God had commanded one place of sacrifice (Leviticus 17:8–9). The principle remains: God's people must worship "in the way God commanded, in a way that pleased Him." (enduringword.com)

**v. 17 — "'Was not the sin of Peor enough for us…?'"**
- At Peor (Numbers 25), Israelite men committed sexual immorality with Moabite women and worshipped Baal of Peor. God sent a plague killing 24,000. This was especially meaningful to Phinehas, who had personally stopped that plague by his zeal (Numbers 25:6–9). (enduringword.com)
- Gill: The sin of Peor "was that so small a sin, that another must be added to it?" — the new altar seemed designed for *continuing* idolatrous worship, not a single act. (studylight.org, Gill)

**v. 18 — "'…if you rebel today against the LORD, tomorrow He will be angry with the whole congregation of Israel.'"**
- The western tribes understood corporate solidarity: the sin of a few brings judgment on all. Grant's Commentary notes: "This is a solemn lesson for the Church of God too…'if one member suffers all the members suffer with it' (1 Corinthians 12:26)." (studylight.org, Grant)

**v. 19 — "'If indeed the land of your inheritance is unclean, then cross over to the land of the LORD's possession…'"**
- This is the "stunning sacrifice" (Guzik): the western tribes offer to give up their own land to make room for the eastern tribes, rather than see them fall into apostasy. "God’s people should do more than simply tell their brethren to stop sinning; they should be willing to pay a price to help their brethren walk rightly." (enduringword.com)
- Gill: "They were willing to quit possession of their own, and make room for them…even though they straitened themselves…which was a brave, noble, spirit indeed." (studylight.org, Gill)

**v. 20 — "'Was not Achan son of Zerah unfaithful…bringing wrath upon the whole congregation…?'"**
- A second example of corporate judgment: one man's sin (Joshua 7) brought defeat at Ai and the death of 36 men. "That man did not perish alone in his iniquity." If one man's sin brought such judgment, the apostasy of 2½ tribes might destroy the nation. (enduringword.com; studylight.org, Gill)
- Dr. Constable (quoted in search results): Achan's example proved that "the sin of one or of a few can bring God's judgment upon all the community." (studylight.org, Constable)

---

### vv. 21–23: The Eastern Tribes' Response

**v. 21 — "Then the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh answered…"**
- The eastern tribes respond to "the heads of the thousands of Israel" — the princes of the respective tribes. (studylight.org, Gill)

**v. 22 — "'The LORD, the Mighty One, is God! The LORD, the Mighty One, is God! He knows, and may Israel also know.'"**
- This is "a most solemn oath" (Whedon). The three Hebrew names *El Elohim Yahweh* "are the three principal names by which the supreme God was known among the Hebrews" (Clarke, quoted at Enduring Word). Hess notes it "can also be translated by the superlative 'The LORD is the greatest God'." (enduringword.com)
- David Guzik: "When believers are misunderstood, their first refuge is God. He knows the heart." (enduringword.com)

**v. 23 — "'If we have built for ourselves an altar to turn away from Him…may the LORD Himself hold us accountable.'"**
- The eastern tribes "recognized the rightness of what the others were doing in challenging" them. They agree with the principle: if they were truly rebellious, they deserved judgment. (enduringword.com)
- Francis Schaeffer (quoted at Enduring Word): "They agreed that if they were worshiping another god or rebelling against God…they deserved judgment…. There was no accommodation of relativism, no Hegelian synthesis, no compromise with truth." (enduringword.com)

---

### vv. 24–29: The Explanation: An Altar of Witness, Not Sacrifice

**v. 24 — "'But in fact we have done this for fear that in the future your descendants might say to ours, "What have you to do with the LORD, the God of Israel?"'"**
- The eastern tribes recognized the Jordan River as a natural barrier that could, over time, become a *spiritual* barrier. Their fear was that future generations west of Jordan would exclude the eastern tribes from the covenant community. (enduringword.com; studylight.org, Gill)

**v. 25 — "'For the LORD has made the Jordan a border between us and you Reubenites and Gadites. You have no share in the LORD!'"**
- The Jordan was the visible, God-ordained boundary. The eastern tribes feared this geographic separation would lead to religious exclusion — that their children would be told they had "no part in the LORD." (enduringword.com)

**v. 26 — "'That is why we said, "Let us take action and build an altar for ourselves, but not for burnt offerings or sacrifices."'"**
- The Pulpit Commentary distinguishes "burnt offering" (whole victim consumed) from "sacrifice" (part offered, part eaten). (biblehub.com, Pulpit)
- Ellicott: the Hebrew is "the altar" — specifically the pattern or copy of the altar of Jehovah, to prove the 2½ tribes had "the same right to approach Him as all the rest." (biblehub.com, Ellicott)

**v. 27 — "'Rather, let it be a witness between us and you and the generations to come, that we will worship the LORD in His presence…'"**
- The altar was not for independent worship but a *memorial* to link the two segments of the nation. The eastern tribes would still travel to Shiloh to offer their real sacrifices. (enduringword.com)
- The Pulpit Commentary: "But that it may be a witness. Rather, for this altar is a witness before Him. Literally, before His face; in the tabernacle, that is, where His special presence was enshrined." (biblehub.com, Pulpit)

**v. 28 — "'…Look at the replica of the altar of the LORD that our fathers made, not for burnt offerings or sacrifices, but as a witness between us and you.'"**
- The Pulpit Commentary: "The existence of an exact reproduction of the altar in Shiloh, erected on Canaanitish ground by the two and a half tribes before their departure across Jordan, was an incontestible proof of their original connection with Israel." The fact that they built it *not on their own territory* but on the western side was "proof positive that it was not intended to be used in contravention of the precepts of the law." (biblehub.com, Pulpit)
- Ellicott draws a contemporary application: "There are many other 'altars' so called in the present day, also an occasion of dispute; and it would tend greatly to peace…if we could be assured that, like this altar, they are 'not for sacrifice' but for a witness to that common worship of Christ as God which is an essential feature of Christianity." (biblehub.com, Ellicott)

**v. 29 — "'Far be it from us to rebel against the LORD…by building an altar…other than the altar of the LORD our God, which stands before His tabernacle.'"**
- The eastern tribes reaffirm their complete agreement with the theological concern of the western delegation. There is only one legitimate altar of sacrifice, and it stands before the tabernacle. (enduringword.com)

---

### vv. 30–31: The Explanation Is Accepted

**v. 30 — "When Phinehas the priest and the chiefs…heard what the descendants of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh had to say, they were satisfied."**
- David Guzik: "Phinehas…deserves credit for being willing to believe his brothers. Phinehas put himself in the place of the eastern tribes and could see that their explanation made sense." (enduringword.com)

**v. 31 — "'Today we know that the LORD is among us, because you have not committed this breach of faith against Him. Consequently, you have delivered the Israelites from the hand of the LORD.'"**
- Phinehas perceived that far from being an act of rebellion, the altar was "a confirmation of the unity of all Israel rather than a tragic declaration of division." (studylight.org, Grant)
- The phrase "delivered the Israelites from the hand of the LORD" means they prevented God's judgment from falling on the nation. (enduringword.com)

---

### vv. 32–34: Resolution and Naming of the Altar

**v. 32 — "Then Phinehas…together with the other leaders, returned to the Israelites in the land of Canaan and brought back a report…"**
- The delegation returned from Gilead to Canaan to report their findings. (enduringword.com)

**v. 33 — "The Israelites were satisfied with the report, and they blessed God and spoke no more about going to war against them…"**
- What could have been a tragic civil war ended in praise to God. "They blessed God" — their first response to good news about their brethren was worship. The Pulpit Commentary notes that "they did not intend" (Hebrew: "they did not say to go up against them") — they formally decided against war. (enduringword.com; biblehub.com, Ellicott/Pulpit)
- The Layman's Bible Commentary: "The story illustrates the foibles of human nature. How easily people misinterpret the motives of others! How quickly they turn from warm comradeship…to suspicion and bitter hostility! It counsels us to be slow to judge and quick to investigate." (studylight.org, Layman's)

**v. 34 — "So the Reubenites and Gadites named the altar Witness, for they said, 'It is a witness between us that the LORD is God.'"**
- The Hebrew word is *Ed* ("witness"). The Pulpit Commentary notes the Arabic name of a nearby site, "the ascent of the father of Ayd," bears a close resemblance to this Hebrew word. (biblehub.com, Pulpit)
- Ellicott: "That the LORD (i.e., Jehovah) is God (of all the twelve tribes alike)." The altar's ultimate testimony is to the unity of God's people under one LORD. (biblehub.com, Ellicott)
- David Guzik closes with seven principles for handling conflict from this chapter: concern for holiness, directness, courageous love, willingness to reconcile before fighting, sacrifice to help, seeing the other person's perspective, and deciding to believe the best. (enduringword.com)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

From the sources I could access, the major interpretive **agreement** on this chapter across traditions is striking. The core reading — dismissal of the faithful eastern tribes; an altar built as a witness, not for sacrifice; misunderstanding leading to near-civil war; Phinehas leading a fact-finding delegation; peaceful resolution — is essentially uniform across Gill (Baptist), the Pulpit Commentary (Anglican), Ellicott (Anglican), David Guzik/Enduring Word (charismatic/Pentecostal), Grant's Commentary (Plymouth Brethren), and the general evangelical sources at Precept Austin.

**Points of emphasis that differ by tradition:**

- **Charismatic/Pentecostal (Enduring Word):** David Guzik heavily emphasises practical application for church life — conflict resolution principles, "hearing God" as the first step (a Pentecostal emphasis), and the need for the Spirit's power to live out the commands. The altar is treated primarily as a lesson in handling misunderstandings. (enduringword.com)

- **Baptist (Gill, Garner-Howes):** Gill focuses on precise historical detail — the length of time involved (fourteen years per Jewish tradition), the geography of the altar's location, and the legal basis in Deuteronomy 13. The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary stresses "cool heads" and the danger of acting on rumour (citing Proverbs 26:20–22), and notes that both sides made mistakes — the eastern tribes for acting "without explanation" and the western tribes for "hastily jumping to conclusions." (studylight.org, Gill and Garner-Howes)

- **Reformed/Anglican (Pulpit, Ellicott):** The Pulpit Commentary uniquely defends the historical reliability of the narrative, arguing that the Israelites' sudden zeal only makes sense after recent victories, and that this internal consistency is evidence for the book's genuineness. It also engages with 19th-century critical scholarship (e.g., Knobel's "destructive criticism"). Ellicott makes an ecumenical application: other Christian "altars" (denominations) should be tolerated if they are "not for sacrifice" but for witness to Christ. (biblehub.com, Pulpit and Ellicott)

- **Plymouth Brethren (Grant):** Grant stresses the typological significance: the one altar speaks of Christ, and any rival altar is rebellion. He also emphasises the corporate nature of the Church: "the Church is 'one body', and 'if one member suffers all the members suffer with it' (1 Corinthians 12:26)." (studylight.org, Grant)

- **Dispensational/Evangelical (Constable):** Dr. Constable notes that God had *not* ordered this altar as He had the memorial stones at Gilgal and the altar on Mount Ebal, and that God had already made provision for unity through the three annual feasts. This makes the altar an act of human initiative, not divine command — well-intentioned but potentially risky. (studylight.org, Constable, via search results)

---

## Other Views

I was unable to access the specifically Catholic, Orthodox, or modern critical scholarship sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) due to search and fetch limits. However, one note from the Pulpit Commentary engages with Josephus, who placed the altar on the *east* side of Jordan — contrary to the Hebrew text which the Pulpit Commentary says places it on the west side. The Pulpit Commentary responds: "Josephus is not infallible, and the Hebrew text seems to assert the very opposite of what he says." (biblehub.com, Pulpit)

---

## Summary of the Chapter (from the sources)

The chapter falls into two halves: (1) an honourable discharge of faithful soldiers (vv. 1–9), and (2) a near-catastrophic misunderstanding resolved through godly confrontation and humble explanation (vv. 10–34). The altar, named *Ed* ("Witness"), was never meant for sacrifice — only to testify that the tribes separated by the Jordan worshipped the same LORD. The western tribes' zeal for holiness, combined with their willingness to investigate before attacking, models conflict resolution among God's people.
